anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.front: List the red flags for back pain.
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.back: Cauda equina (saddle anaesthesia, bladder/bowel, bilateral sciatica), malignancy (age >50, weight loss, night pain, past cancer), infection (fever, IVDU, immunosuppression), fracture (trauma, osteoporosis, steroids), and inflammatory (young, morning stiffness >30 min, better with exercise).

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.front: In which direction does a disc usually herniate, and why?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.back: Posterolaterally — the posterior longitudinal ligament reinforces the disc centrally, so the weak point is posterolateral (where it compresses the nerve root).

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.front: Which nerve root does an L4/L5 disc prolapse typically compress, and what is the deficit?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.back: The L5 root (the traversing root) → weak big-toe/great-toe extension (EHL), numb dorsum of foot, difficulty heel-walking.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.front: Which nerve root does an L5/S1 disc prolapse typically compress, and what is the deficit?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.back: The S1 root → weak plantarflexion, numb sole/lateral foot, and a reduced ankle jerk.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.front: Why does a paracentral disc hit the LOWER (traversing) nerve root rather than the exiting one?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.back: The exiting root has already left above the disc; the traversing root (destined to exit at the level below) crosses the posterolateral disc and is compressed — so an L4/5 disc affects L5.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.front: What is sciatica, and which test reproduces it?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.back: Radicular leg pain in a dermatomal (L5/S1) distribution; the straight-leg-raise (Lasègue’s) test reproduces it by stretching the sciatic nerve.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.front: At what level does the spinal cord end, and what lies below it?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.back: At L1/L2 (the conus medullaris); below it the cauda equina (the lumbosacral nerve roots) floats in CSF.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.front: What are the red-flag features of cauda equina syndrome?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.back: Saddle anaesthesia, painless urinary retention (then overflow incontinence), faecal incontinence / loss of anal tone, and bilateral sciatica & leg weakness.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.front: How is suspected cauda equina syndrome managed?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.back: It is a surgical emergency — urgent MRI and decompression; delay risks permanent bladder, bowel & sexual dysfunction.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.front: Contrast the motor signs of a cord (UMN) lesion with a cauda equina (LMN) lesion.
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.back: A cord lesion → UMN signs below the level (spastic, hyperreflexic, up-going plantars, a sensory level); cauda equina → LMN signs (flaccid, areflexic, down-going plantars, saddle/root sensory loss).

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.front: What are the features of malignant spinal cord compression?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.back: Back pain, a sensory level, UMN signs below and bladder involvement → urgent MRI whole spine and steroids (a metastatic emergency).

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.front: Describe an osteoporotic wedge (compression) fracture.
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.back: Loss of anterior vertebral height from axial/flexion load in weakened bone (elderly, steroids); usually stable and treated conservatively.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.front: What is a burst fracture, and why can it be dangerous?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.back: An axial-loading fracture with retropulsion of bone into the spinal canal — potentially unstable, risking cord/cauda injury.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.front: What is a Chance fracture?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.back: A flexion-distraction (“seat-belt”) fracture through the vertebral body & posterior elements; often associated with intra-abdominal injuries.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.front: Define kyphosis, lordosis and scoliosis.
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.back: Kyphosis — excessive thoracic flexion curve; lordosis — excessive lumbar extension curve; scoliosis — lateral curvature with vertebral rotation.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.front: What is spondylolisthesis?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.back: Forward slippage of one vertebra on the one below (commonly L5 on S1) — may cause back pain & radiculopathy.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.front: What is spinal stenosis, and its classic symptom?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.back: Narrowing of the spinal canal (degenerative/spondylotic) → neurogenic claudication (leg pain on walking, relieved by flexion/sitting).

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.front: At what vertebral level is a lumbar puncture performed, and why there?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.back: At L3/L4 or L4/L5 — below the conus (L1/2), so the needle meets only mobile cauda equina roots rather than the cord.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.front: What is Tuffier's line?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.back: A line joining the iliac crests, crossing the L4 spinous process (≈ the L4/5 interspace) — the landmark for a lumbar puncture.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.front: List, in order, the layers pierced during a lumbar puncture to reach CSF.
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.back: Skin → superficial fascia → supraspinous ligament → interspinous ligament → ligamentum flavum → epidural space → dura → arachnoid → subarachnoid space (CSF).

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.front: What is the difference between spinal and epidural anaesthesia?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.back: Spinal injects into the subarachnoid space (CSF) (dural puncture); epidural injects into the epidural (extradural) space (no dural puncture).

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.front: Distinguish spina bifida occulta, meningocele and myelomeningocele.
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.back: Occulta — failed vertebral arch fusion only (hair tuft/dimple, usually asymptomatic); meningocele — meninges herniate (cord normal); myelomeningocele — meninges and neural tissue herniate → deficit (± Chiari II & hydrocephalus).

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.front: How are neural tube defects prevented and screened for?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.back: Prevented by peri-conceptional folic acid; screened by a raised maternal serum AFP (and ultrasound).

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.front: What does the straight-leg-raise test assess, and the femoral stretch test?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.back: SLR stretches the sciatic nerve → L5/S1 radiculopathy; the femoral stretch (prone knee flexion) targets the L2–L4 roots (anterior thigh pain).

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.front: Give the root values of the knee and ankle jerks.
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.back: Knee jerk = L3/L4; ankle jerk = S1.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.front: Give dermatome anchors for T4, T10, L1, L5 and S1.
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.back: T4 nipple · T10 umbilicus · L1 groin · L5 big toe/dorsum of foot · S1 little toe/sole.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.front: What does an up-going plantar response indicate?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.back: An upper motor neuron (UMN) lesion (Babinski sign) — pointing to a cord/brain lesion rather than a root/cauda problem.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.front: What suggests inflammatory (rather than mechanical) back pain?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.back: A young patient with insidious pain, morning stiffness >30 min, pain that is better with exercise & worse with rest, and night pain (e.g. ankylosing spondylitis).

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.front: What three columns determine spinal stability (Denis)?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.back: The anterior, middle & posterior columns; involvement of ≥2 columns suggests instability.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.front: How many vertebrae are there, and in what regional distribution?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.back: 33: 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 fused sacral & 4 fused coccygeal (24 mobile presacral).

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.front: Which spinal curvatures are primary, and which secondary?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.back: Primary (kyphotic) — thoracic & sacral (present at birth); secondary (lordotic) — cervical & lumbar (develop after birth with head control & walking).

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.front: What are the components of a typical vertebra?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.back: A body (weight-bearing) and a vertebral arch (pedicles + laminae) enclosing the vertebral foramen, with one spinous, two transverse and paired superior/inferior articular processes.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.front: What is transmitted by the intervertebral foramen?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.back: The spinal nerve (with its dorsal root ganglion) and accompanying radicular vessels; it is narrowed by disc prolapse or osteophytes → radiculopathy.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.front: What feature is unique to cervical vertebrae?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.back: The foramen transversarium in each transverse process — transmitting the vertebral artery (C1–C6); cervical vertebrae also have bifid spinous processes (C3–6).

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.front: What distinguishes thoracic vertebrae?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.back: A heart-shaped body with costal facets/demifacets (for rib heads) and transverse costal facets (for rib tubercles), plus a long, downward-pointing spinous process.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.front: What distinguishes lumbar vertebrae?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.back: A large, kidney-shaped body, no costal facets or transverse foramina, a short blunt (“hatchet”) spinous process and a mamillary process.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.front: Describe the atlas (C1).
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.back: It has no body and no spinous process — just anterior & posterior arches and lateral masses; its superior facets articulate with the occipital condyles.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.front: Describe the axis (C2).
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.back: It bears the dens (odontoid process), which projects up as a pivot for the atlas to rotate around.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.front: What is the vertebra prominens?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.back: C7 — it has a long, non-bifid spinous process that is a palpable surface landmark.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.front: Name the key features of the sacrum.
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.back: 5 fused vertebrae; the sacral promontory, ala, anterior & posterior sacral foramina, median crest, and the sacral hiatus (for caudal anaesthesia).

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.front: Classify the intervertebral joints, and describe the disc.
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.back: Secondary cartilaginous (symphyses); the intervertebral disc = an outer annulus fibrosus and inner nucleus pulposus (a shock absorber).

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.front: What are the uncovertebral joints (of Luschka)?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.back: Small clefts on the lateral margins of the cervical vertebral bodies; they can develop osteophytes that narrow the intervertebral foramen.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.front: Classify the zygapophyseal (facet) joints.
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.back: Synovial plane joints between the superior & inferior articular processes of adjacent vertebrae.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.front: How does facet orientation determine regional movement?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.back: Cervical — oblique (all movements); thoracic — coronal (rotation, limited by ribs); lumbar — sagittal (flexion/extension, little rotation).

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.front: What movement occurs at the atlanto-occipital joint?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.back: Flexion & extension — nodding the head (“YES”).

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.front: What movement occurs at the atlanto-axial joint?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.back: Rotation around the dens — shaking the head (“NO”); it provides ~50% of neck rotation.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.front: What does the transverse ligament of the atlas do?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.back: It holds the dens against the anterior arch of the atlas (part of the cruciate ligament), preventing posterior displacement of the dens onto the cord.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.front: Name the other craniovertebral ligaments.
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.back: The alar ligaments (dens → occipital condyles, limit rotation), the apical ligament, and the tectorial membrane (upward continuation of the PLL).

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.front: Why is transverse ligament rupture or a dens fracture dangerous?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.back: It causes atlanto-axial instability — the dens can compress the spinal cord (potentially fatal); a recognised risk in rheumatoid arthritis and trauma.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.front: What does the anterior longitudinal ligament do?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.back: Runs down the front of the vertebral bodies and is the only spinal ligament to limit extension (it is broad & strong).

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.front: What does the posterior longitudinal ligament do?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.back: Runs down the back of the bodies (within the canal); it limits flexion and, being narrow centrally, directs disc herniation posterolaterally.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.front: What is the ligamentum flavum?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.back: An elastic ligament connecting adjacent laminae; it resists flexion and is the last ligament pierced (before the dura) in a lumbar puncture.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.front: What is the ligamentum nuchae?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.back: The fibroelastic cervical continuation of the supraspinous & interspinous ligaments — a median septum providing muscle attachment and helping support the head.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.front: What is a Jefferson fracture?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.back: A burst fracture of the atlas (C1) ring from axial loading (e.g. diving into shallow water).

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.front: What is a hangman's fracture?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.back: A bilateral fracture through the pars interarticularis/pedicles of C2 (axis) from hyperextension.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.front: What is a cervical rib, and its clinical consequence?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.back: An extra rib arising from C7; it can compress the brachial plexus/subclavian vessels → thoracic outlet syndrome.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.front: What are sacralisation and lumbarisation?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.back: Transitional vertebral anomalies at the L5/S1 junction — sacralisation (L5 fuses to the sacrum) or lumbarisation (S1 becomes a separate lumbar-like vertebra).

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.front: Which regions of the spine are most mobile, and which is splinted?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.back: The cervical & lumbar regions are the most mobile; the thoracic spine is splinted by the ribs.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Muscles & Movemen.front: What is the fundamental difference between the extrinsic and intrinsic back muscles?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Muscles & Movemen.back: Extrinsic muscles move the upper limb / ribs and are supplied by anterior rami (or CN XI); intrinsic (true) muscles move the vertebral column and are supplied by posterior (dorsal) rami.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Muscles & Movemen.front: Which single rule defines the intrinsic (true) back muscles?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Muscles & Movemen.back: They are all supplied by the posterior (dorsal) rami of spinal nerves.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Muscles & Movemen.front: Name the superficial extrinsic back muscles.
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Muscles & Movemen.back: Trapezius, latissimus dorsi, levator scapulae and the rhomboids (major & minor) — all move the upper limb.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Muscles & Movemen.front: What is the nerve supply and action of trapezius?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Muscles & Movemen.back: Motor from the accessory nerve (CN XI) (+ C3–4 proprioception); it elevates, retracts & rotates the scapula.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Muscles & Movemen.front: What is the nerve supply and action of latissimus dorsi?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Muscles & Movemen.back: The thoracodorsal nerve (C6–8); it extends, adducts & medially rotates the arm (the “hand in the back pocket” muscle).

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Muscles & Movemen.front: Which nerve supplies the rhomboids and levator scapulae?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Muscles & Movemen.back: The dorsal scapular nerve (C4–5 for the rhomboids; C5 + C3–4 for levator scapulae).

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Muscles & Movemen.front: What is the function of the serratus posterior muscles?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Muscles & Movemen.back: They are accessory muscles of respiration (supplied by intercostal nerves) — an intermediate extrinsic layer.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Muscles & Movemen.front: Why are the extrinsic muscles supplied by anterior rami despite lying on the back?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Muscles & Movemen.back: They are limb/thoracic muscles that migrated onto the back during development, so they retain their ventral (anterior ramus) innervation — trapezius (CN XI) is the exception.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Muscles & Movemen.front: Name the three intrinsic muscle layers and a representative of each.
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Muscles & Movemen.back: Superficial — splenius (capitis/cervicis); intermediate — erector spinae; deep — transversospinalis (semispinalis, multifidus, rotatores).

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Muscles & Movemen.front: Name the three columns of erector spinae from lateral to medial.
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Muscles & Movemen.back: Iliocostalis (lateral), Longissimus (intermediate), Spinalis (medial) — “I Love Spaghetti.”

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Muscles & Movemen.front: Where does erector spinae originate, and what is its main action?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Muscles & Movemen.back: From a common tendon on the sacrum, iliac crest & lumbar spinous processes; it is the main extensor of the spine (bilateral) and a lateral flexor (unilateral).

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Muscles & Movemen.front: Describe the fibre direction and action of the transversospinalis group.
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Muscles & Movemen.back: Fibres run obliquely from transverse processes up to spinous processes; they extend and rotate the spine to the opposite side, and stabilise it.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Muscles & Movemen.front: Which transversospinalis muscle is the key lumbar stabiliser?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Muscles & Movemen.back: Multifidus — a major segmental stabiliser targeted in back-pain rehabilitation.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Muscles & Movemen.front: What are the actions of splenius capitis and cervicis?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Muscles & Movemen.back: Bilaterally they extend the head/neck; unilaterally they rotate the head to the same side.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Muscles & Movemen.front: Name the four suboccipital muscles.
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Muscles & Movemen.back: Rectus capitis posterior major & minor and obliquus capitis superior & inferior.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Muscles & Movemen.front: What are the borders of the suboccipital triangle?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Muscles & Movemen.back: Rectus capitis posterior major (medial), obliquus capitis superior (lateral) and obliquus capitis inferior (inferior).

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Muscles & Movemen.front: What are the contents of the suboccipital triangle?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Muscles & Movemen.back: The third part of the vertebral artery and the suboccipital nerve (posterior ramus of C1), within the suboccipital venous plexus.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Muscles & Movemen.front: What nerve supplies the suboccipital muscles?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Muscles & Movemen.back: The suboccipital nerve — the posterior ramus of C1.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Muscles & Movemen.front: Why is the vertebral artery vulnerable in the suboccipital region?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Muscles & Movemen.back: Its third part lies in the floor of the triangle on the posterior arch of the atlas before entering the foramen magnum — at risk in extreme neck rotation or manipulation (dissection).

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Muscles & Movemen.front: Which muscles chiefly EXTEND the vertebral column?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Muscles & Movemen.back: The erector spinae, transversospinalis and (in the neck) splenius — all intrinsic, dorsal-rami muscles.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Muscles & Movemen.front: Which muscles chiefly FLEX the vertebral column?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Muscles & Movemen.back: The anterior abdominal wall (rectus abdominis, obliques) and the psoas major — the intrinsic back muscles are extensors, not flexors.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Muscles & Movemen.front: In which region is rotation of the spine freest, and why?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Muscles & Movemen.back: The thoracic region — its coronally-oriented facet joints favour rotation (though the ribs limit total range).

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Muscles & Movemen.front: What is the thoracolumbar fascia, and its significance?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Muscles & Movemen.back: A strong fascial sheet enclosing the deep back muscles; it gives attachment to latissimus dorsi & transversus abdominis, transferring load between the trunk and limb.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Muscles & Movemen.front: What is the commonest cause of acute back pain?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Muscles & Movemen.back: Mechanical back strain — of the erector spinae muscles and spinal ligaments.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Muscles & Movemen.front: What is whiplash?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Muscles & Movemen.back: A hyperextension–flexion injury (e.g. rear-end collision) that strains the cervical muscles & ligaments.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Muscles & Movemen.front: What deficit follows accessory nerve (CN XI) injury?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Muscles & Movemen.back: Trapezius palsy → a drooping shoulder, weakness of shoulder elevation/scapular retraction (e.g. after posterior triangle/lymph-node surgery).

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Muscles & Movemen.front: How does the semispinalis differ from multifidus and rotatores?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Muscles & Movemen.back: By the number of segments spanned: semispinalis ~6, multifidus ~2–4, rotatores 1–2 — all part of transversospinalis.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Muscles & Movemen.front: What movement combination do the suboccipital muscles produce?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Muscles & Movemen.back: Extension & rotation of the head at the craniovertebral (atlanto-occipital & atlanto-axial) joints — fine postural adjustment.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Spinal Cord & Men.front: Where does the spinal cord begin and end in an adult?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Spinal Cord & Men.back: From the foramen magnum to the conus medullaris at L1/L2 (it ends lower in neonates).

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Spinal Cord & Men.front: What are the two cord enlargements, and what do they serve?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Spinal Cord & Men.back: The cervical enlargement (C5–T1) for the upper limb (brachial plexus) and the lumbosacral enlargement (L1–S3) for the lower limb.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Spinal Cord & Men.front: What is the filum terminale?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Spinal Cord & Men.back: A pial strand from the conus medullaris: the filum terminale internum descends to the dural sac at S2, then the dural-invested filum terminale externum anchors to the coccyx.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Spinal Cord & Men.front: How many pairs of spinal nerves are there, and in what distribution?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Spinal Cord & Men.back: 31 pairs: 8 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral & 1 coccygeal.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Spinal Cord & Men.front: Explain how cervical spinal nerves exit relative to their pedicles.
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Spinal Cord & Men.back: C1–C7 exit ABOVE their correspondingly-numbered pedicle; C8 exits below the C7 pedicle; thereafter each nerve exits below its numbered pedicle.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Spinal Cord & Men.front: What is contained in the dorsal, ventral and lateral horns of grey matter?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Spinal Cord & Men.back: Dorsal horn — sensory neurons; ventral horn — motor (LMN) cell bodies; lateral horn (T1–L2) — sympathetic preganglionic neurons.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Spinal Cord & Men.front: Where are the sensory neuron cell bodies located?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Spinal Cord & Men.back: In the dorsal root ganglion (DRG) on the dorsal root.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Spinal Cord & Men.front: What do the dorsal and ventral roots carry, and what do they form?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Spinal Cord & Men.back: The dorsal root is sensory (with the DRG) and the ventral root is motor; they unite to form the mixed spinal nerve.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Spinal Cord & Men.front: Into what does each spinal nerve divide, and what do they supply?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Spinal Cord & Men.back: A posterior (dorsal) ramus (deep back muscles & overlying skin) and a larger anterior (ventral) ramus (limbs & body wall, forming plexuses).

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Spinal Cord & Men.front: Name the three spinal meninges from outer to inner.
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Spinal Cord & Men.back: Dura mater (tough outer), arachnoid mater (middle), pia mater (adherent to the cord).

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Spinal Cord & Men.front: At what level does the dural sac (and subarachnoid space) end?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Spinal Cord & Men.back: At S2.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Spinal Cord & Men.front: What are the denticulate ligaments?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Spinal Cord & Men.back: Lateral extensions of pia mater that anchor the cord to the dura, suspending it within the subarachnoid space.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Spinal Cord & Men.front: What does the epidural (extradural) space contain?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Spinal Cord & Men.back: Fat and the internal vertebral venous (Batson’s) plexus — the target for epidural anaesthesia.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Spinal Cord & Men.front: Where is CSF found, and where is it sampled?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Spinal Cord & Men.back: In the subarachnoid space; it is sampled from the lumbar cistern (L2–S2) below the conus (lumbar puncture).

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Spinal Cord & Men.front: What does the dorsal column–medial lemniscus (DCML) tract carry, and where does it decussate?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Spinal Cord & Men.back: Fine touch, vibration & proprioception; it decussates in the medulla (as the internal arcuate fibres).

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Spinal Cord & Men.front: What does the spinothalamic tract carry, and where does it decussate?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Spinal Cord & Men.back: Pain, temperature & crude touch; it decussates at the cord level (within ~1–2 segments, via the anterior white commissure).

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Spinal Cord & Men.front: Why does a cord hemisection give ipsilateral touch loss but contralateral pain loss?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Spinal Cord & Men.back: Because DCML crosses high (medulla) — so touch/proprioception loss is ipsilateral — whereas spinothalamic crosses low (at the cord) — so pain/temperature loss is contralateral (the basis of Brown-Séquard syndrome).

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Spinal Cord & Men.front: Describe the corticospinal (pyramidal) tract.
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Spinal Cord & Men.back: The voluntary motor pathway; ~85% decussate in the medullary pyramids to form the lateral corticospinal tract.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Spinal Cord & Men.front: Contrast an upper and lower motor neuron lesion.
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Spinal Cord & Men.back: UMN (above the anterior horn) → spasticity, hyperreflexia, up-going plantars, minimal wasting; LMN (anterior horn/root/nerve) → flaccid, wasted, areflexic, fasciculations.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Spinal Cord & Men.front: Describe the arterial supply of the spinal cord.
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Spinal Cord & Men.back: One anterior spinal artery (anterior ⅔ of the cord) and two posterior spinal arteries (posterior ⅓ / dorsal columns), from the vertebral arteries, reinforced by segmental radicular arteries.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Spinal Cord & Men.front: What is the artery of Adamkiewicz?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Spinal Cord & Men.back: The largest anterior segmental medullary (radicular) artery, usually arising on the left around T9–T12 — a major supply to the lower thoracic/lumbar cord.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Spinal Cord & Men.front: Which region of the cord is a watershed zone, and why does it matter?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Spinal Cord & Men.back: The mid-thoracic cord (~T4–T9) — vulnerable to ischaemia (e.g. during aortic cross-clamping/surgery).

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Spinal Cord & Men.front: What is anterior spinal artery syndrome?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Spinal Cord & Men.back: Infarction of the anterior ⅔ of the cord → bilateral loss of motor (corticospinal) and pain/temperature (spinothalamic) below the level, with preserved dorsal-column (touch/proprioception) function.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Spinal Cord & Men.front: What are the features of Brown-Séquard (cord hemisection) syndrome?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Spinal Cord & Men.back: Ipsilateral motor & dorsal-column (touch/proprioception) loss, plus contralateral pain/temperature loss (beginning a few segments below the lesion).

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Spinal Cord & Men.front: What is subacute combined degeneration of the cord?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Spinal Cord & Men.back: Vitamin B12 deficiency damaging the dorsal columns & lateral corticospinal tracts → sensory ataxia + UMN weakness.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Spinal Cord & Men.front: What is tabes dorsalis?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Spinal Cord & Men.back: Degeneration of the dorsal columns in tertiary syphilis → sensory ataxia, loss of proprioception & a positive Romberg sign.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Spinal Cord & Men.front: What is central cord syndrome (and the syringomyelia pattern)?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Spinal Cord & Men.back: Injury to the central cord (often hyperextension in the elderly) → upper-limb > lower-limb weakness; syringomyelia gives a “cape” loss of pain/temperature.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Spinal Cord & Men.front: Where are the sympathetic preganglionic neurons of the cord located?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Spinal Cord & Men.back: In the lateral horn of grey matter, T1–L2 (the thoracolumbar outflow).

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Vessels.front: Which arteries provide the segmental spinal supply in each region?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Vessels.back: Cervical — vertebral & ascending cervical; thoracic — posterior intercostal; lumbar — lumbar arteries; sacral — lateral & median sacral arteries.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Vessels.front: What does each segmental artery supply?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Vessels.back: The vertebral body & periosteum (and back muscles/skin), plus a spinal branch that enters the intervertebral foramen to supply the vertebra, meninges and (via radicular arteries) the roots & cord.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Vessels.front: What enters the intervertebral foramen from each segmental artery?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Vessels.back: A spinal branch, which gives radicular arteries (to the nerve roots) and, at some levels, a segmental medullary artery (which reaches and reinforces the cord’s longitudinal arteries), plus a branch to the vertebral body.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Vessels.front: Describe the three longitudinal arteries of the spinal cord.
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Vessels.back: One anterior spinal artery (from the vertebral arteries) supplying the anterior ⅔, and two posterior spinal arteries (from the vertebral arteries/PICA) supplying the posterior ⅓ (dorsal columns).

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Vessels.front: What is the artery of Adamkiewicz?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Vessels.back: The largest anterior segmental medullary (radicular) artery, usually arising on the left around T9–T12 — the major feeder of the lower thoracic/lumbar cord.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Vessels.front: Which region of the cord is a watershed, and why does it matter?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Vessels.back: The mid-thoracic cord (~T4–T9) — poorly reinforced, so it is vulnerable to ischaemia during aortic surgery or hypotension.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Vessels.front: What is anterior spinal artery syndrome?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Vessels.back: Infarction of the anterior ⅔ of the cord (e.g. aortic cross-clamp, Adamkiewicz injury) → bilateral motor & pain/temperature loss with preserved dorsal columns (proprioception).

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Vessels.front: Name the two vertebral venous plexuses and their locations.
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Vessels.back: The internal vertebral venous plexus (in the epidural space, around the dura) and the external vertebral venous plexus (outside the vertebral column).

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Vessels.front: What are the basivertebral veins?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Vessels.back: Veins that emerge from the posterior surface of the vertebral body, draining it into the internal vertebral venous plexus.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Vessels.front: How does the cord itself drain venously?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Vessels.back: Via anterior & posterior spinal veins into the internal vertebral venous plexus, then out through intervertebral veins to the segmental veins (azygos, lumbar, etc.).

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Vessels.front: What is clinically important about Batson's vertebral venous plexus?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Vessels.back: It is valveless and communicates freely with the pelvic, abdominal & thoracic veins — a route for prostate & breast cancer (and pelvic infection) to spread to the vertebrae, pelvis & brain, bypassing the caval/pulmonary filter.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Vessels.front: Why do raised intra-abdominal/thoracic pressures divert blood into Batson's plexus?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Vessels.back: Because the plexus is valveless, increased pressure (coughing, straining, tumour) pushes blood retrogradely into the vertebral veins — carrying tumour cells to the spine.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Vessels.front: Which cancers classically metastasise to the spine via Batson's plexus?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Vessels.back: Prostate and breast cancer (also lung, kidney, thyroid) — the vertebrae are a very common site of bony metastasis.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Vessels.front: Describe the course of the vertebral artery.
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Vessels.back: A branch of the subclavian artery; it ascends through the foramina transversaria of C6→C1, crosses the suboccipital triangle, and passes through the foramen magnum to unite as the basilar artery.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Vessels.front: What does the vertebral artery supply, and what is a key risk?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Vessels.back: It gives the anterior & posterior spinal arteries and PICA, and supplies the posterior brain circulation; dissection (neck trauma/manipulation) → posterior circulation stroke.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Vessels.front: How does spinal cord ischaemia complicate aortic surgery?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Vessels.back: Thoracoabdominal aortic surgery/aneurysm repair can occlude the artery of Adamkiewicz → anterior cord infarction & paraplegia.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Vessels.front: Why is less local anaesthetic needed for an epidural in pregnancy?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Vessels.back: Epidural venous engorgement (from IVC compression) reduces the epidural space volume, so a smaller dose of anaesthetic spreads further.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Vessels.front: What can cause an epidural (extradural) haematoma in the spine?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Vessels.back: Bleeding from the internal vertebral venous plexus (or an epidural artery) into the epidural space, which can compress the cord.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Vessels.front: From what does the anterior spinal artery arise, and where does it run?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Vessels.back: From the two vertebral arteries (which unite); it runs in the anterior median fissure of the cord.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Vessels.front: Which vessels reinforce the longitudinal spinal arteries along the cord?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Vessels.back: The segmental medullary (radicular) arteries — branches of the spinal branches of the segmental arteries — the largest being the artery of Adamkiewicz.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.question: A large central lumbar disc prolapse causing saddle anaesthesia, painless urinary retention and bilateral sciatica indicates:
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.explanation: This triad (saddle anaesthesia, bladder dysfunction, bilateral sciatica) is cauda equina syndrome — a surgical emergency requiring urgent MRI and decompression.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.question: An L4/L5 disc prolapse most commonly compresses which nerve root?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.explanation: A paracentral L4/5 disc compresses the traversing L5 root (the exiting L4 root has already left above the disc).

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.question: Weak plantarflexion and a reduced ankle jerk suggest compression of which root (and which disc)?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.explanation: The S1 root (typically an L5/S1 disc) supplies plantarflexion and the ankle jerk; its compression weakens plantarflexion and reduces the ankle reflex.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.question: Intervertebral discs most commonly herniate in which direction?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.explanation: Discs herniate posterolaterally because the posterior longitudinal ligament reinforces the midline; this is where the traversing nerve root is compressed.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.question: The spinal cord (conus medullaris) usually ends at which vertebral level in adults?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.explanation: The adult spinal cord ends at L1/L2 as the conus medullaris; below this the cauda equina roots descend within the subarachnoid space.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.question: A lumbar puncture is performed at L3/4 or L4/5 primarily because:
options: It is below the conus medullaris, so the needle avoids the cord
There is no CSF higher up
The ligamentum flavum is absent there
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.explanation: LP is done below the conus (L1/2) so the needle enters CSF among the mobile cauda equina roots rather than risking the spinal cord.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.question: Tuffier's line, joining the iliac crests, crosses which spinous process?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.explanation: Tuffier's (the intercristal) line crosses the L4 spinous process (≈ the L4/5 interspace), the landmark for lumbar puncture.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.question: During a midline lumbar puncture, which ligament is pierced immediately before the dura?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.explanation: The order is supraspinous → interspinous → ligamentum flavum → epidural space → dura; the ligamentum flavum is the last ligament before the epidural space and dura.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.question: Spinal (subarachnoid) anaesthesia differs from epidural anaesthesia in that spinal anaesthesia:
options: Uses a larger volume of anaesthetic
Has a slower onset of block than epidural
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.explanation: Spinal anaesthesia is injected through the dura into the CSF (subarachnoid space); epidural anaesthesia is placed in the epidural space without dural puncture.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.question: A cord (upper motor neuron) lesion is distinguished from a cauda equina (lower motor neuron) lesion by:
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.explanation: A cord lesion produces UMN signs below the level (spasticity, hyperreflexia, up-going plantars, a sensory level); cauda equina produces LMN signs (flaccid, areflexic).

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.question: Which feature is a 'red flag' pointing to malignancy as a cause of back pain?
options: Improvement with exercise in a young patient
Age >50 with weight loss and night pain
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.explanation: Age >50, weight loss, unremitting night pain and a history of cancer are red flags for malignant (often metastatic) back pain.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.question: Malignant spinal cord compression is suggested by back pain plus:
options: A sensory level with UMN signs below and bladder involvement
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.explanation: Cord compression gives a sensory level and UMN signs below the lesion with sphincter involvement — an oncological emergency requiring urgent MRI and steroids.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.question: An osteoporotic vertebral fracture is typically which type?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.explanation: Osteoporotic fractures are typically anterior wedge (compression) fractures with loss of anterior vertebral height.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.question: A flexion-distraction 'seat-belt' vertebral fracture is called a:
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.explanation: A Chance fracture is a horizontal flexion-distraction injury through the vertebra, classically from a lap seat-belt and often associated with intra-abdominal injury.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.question: Neurogenic claudication (leg pain on walking, relieved by sitting/flexion) is characteristic of:
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.explanation: Lumbar spinal stenosis causes neurogenic claudication — leg pain/heaviness on walking relieved by flexing forward (which widens the canal).

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.question: A myelomeningocele differs from a meningocele in that a myelomeningocele:
options: Presents identically to a meningocele on examination
Is the same as spina bifida occulta
Contains herniated neural tissue as well as meninges
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.explanation: A myelomeningocele herniates both meninges and neural tissue, causing neurological deficit (and often Chiari II/hydrocephalus); a meningocele contains meninges only.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.question: The ankle jerk reflex tests which nerve root?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.explanation: The ankle jerk is an S1 reflex; the knee jerk is L3/L4.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.question: The straight-leg-raise (Lasègue's) test primarily assesses which nerve roots?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.explanation: SLR stretches the sciatic nerve and reproduces pain from L5/S1 root irritation; the femoral stretch test assesses the higher L2–L4 roots.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.question: The umbilicus corresponds to which dermatome, a useful marker of a sensory level?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.explanation: The umbilicus is the T10 dermatome (nipple T4, groin L1) — helpful for identifying a sensory level in cord lesions.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.question: How many vertebrae are there in total (including fused sacral and coccygeal)?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.explanation: There are 33 vertebrae: 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 fused sacral and 4 fused coccygeal (24 are mobile presacral).

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.question: Which curvatures are the PRIMARY (present at birth) curvatures?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.explanation: The thoracic and sacral (kyphotic) curvatures are primary; the cervical and lumbar (lordotic) curvatures are secondary, developing with head control and walking.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.question: The foramen transversarium, transmitting the vertebral artery, is characteristic of which vertebrae?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.explanation: The foramen transversarium is unique to cervical vertebrae and transmits the vertebral artery (through C1–C6).

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.question: Costal facets (demifacets) on the vertebral body are found on which vertebrae?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.explanation: Thoracic vertebrae have costal facets/demifacets on their bodies (for rib heads) and transverse costal facets (for rib tubercles).

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.question: Which structure is ABSENT in the atlas (C1)?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.explanation: The atlas has no body and no spinous process — it is a ring of anterior and posterior arches with lateral masses.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.question: The dens (odontoid process) is a feature of which vertebra?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.explanation: The dens projects upward from the body of the axis (C2) and serves as the pivot for the atlas.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.question: The intervertebral disc joint is classified as a:
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.explanation: Intervertebral (body-to-body) joints are secondary cartilaginous joints (symphyses); the disc has an outer annulus fibrosus and inner nucleus pulposus.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.question: The zygapophyseal (facet) joints are:
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.explanation: Facet joints between the articular processes are synovial plane joints; their orientation determines the movement permitted in each region.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.question: Nodding the head 'yes' (flexion/extension) occurs mainly at which joint?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.explanation: The atlanto-occipital joint (C0–C1) permits flexion/extension — the 'yes' nod; the atlanto-axial joint permits rotation ('no').

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.question: Rotation of the head ('no') occurs at the atlanto-axial joint, pivoting around the:
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.explanation: The atlanto-axial joint is a pivot: the atlas (and skull) rotate around the dens of the axis, providing about half of neck rotation.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.question: The transverse ligament of the atlas functions to:
options: Hold the dens against the anterior arch of the atlas
Support the head like a strut
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.explanation: The transverse ligament holds the dens against the anterior arch of the atlas; its rupture (e.g. in rheumatoid arthritis) allows the dens to compress the cord.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.question: Which spinal ligament is the only one that limits EXTENSION?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.explanation: The anterior longitudinal ligament, running along the front of the vertebral bodies, is the only spinal ligament that limits extension.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.question: The narrow posterior longitudinal ligament contributes to disc herniation being directed:
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.explanation: Because the PLL reinforces the midline posteriorly, discs herniate posterolaterally, where they compress the traversing nerve root.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.question: The elastic ligament connecting adjacent laminae, pierced last before the dura in a lumbar puncture, is the:
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.explanation: The ligamentum flavum (elastic, between laminae) resists flexion and is the last ligament traversed before the epidural space and dura in an LP.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.question: A burst fracture of the C1 (atlas) ring from axial loading is a:
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.explanation: A Jefferson fracture is a burst fracture of the atlas ring caused by axial loading (e.g. diving into shallow water).

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.question: A bilateral fracture of the C2 pars interarticularis from hyperextension is called a:
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.explanation: A hangman's fracture is a bilateral fracture through the pars interarticularis/pedicles of the axis (C2) from hyperextension.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.question: A cervical rib arises from which vertebra and can cause which syndrome?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.explanation: A cervical rib arises from C7 and can compress the lower brachial plexus/subclavian vessels, causing thoracic outlet syndrome.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.question: Thoracic spine movement is most restricted because it is:
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.explanation: The thoracic spine is splinted by the rib cage and its coronally-oriented facets favour rotation but limit overall mobility, making it the least mobile region.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.question: Which vertebra is the 'vertebra prominens' with a long, non-bifid spinous process used as a surface landmark?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.explanation: C7 is the vertebra prominens; its long, non-bifid spinous process is easily palpated at the base of the neck.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Muscles & Movemen.question: The intrinsic (true) back muscles are all supplied by the:
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Muscles & Movemen.explanation: The defining feature of the intrinsic back muscles is their supply by the posterior (dorsal) rami; extrinsic muscles are supplied by anterior rami.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Muscles & Movemen.question: Which back muscle is supplied by the accessory nerve (CN XI)?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Muscles & Movemen.explanation: Trapezius receives its motor supply from the accessory nerve (CN XI), with C3–4 for proprioception — the classic exception among back muscles.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Muscles & Movemen.question: Latissimus dorsi ('hand in the back pocket' muscle) is supplied by the:
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Muscles & Movemen.explanation: Latissimus dorsi is supplied by the thoracodorsal nerve (C6–8) and extends, adducts and medially rotates the arm.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Muscles & Movemen.question: The rhomboids and levator scapulae are supplied by the:
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Muscles & Movemen.explanation: The dorsal scapular nerve (C4–5) supplies the rhomboids (and contributes to levator scapulae, which also receives C3–4).

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Muscles & Movemen.question: The erector spinae columns from LATERAL to MEDIAL are:
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Muscles & Movemen.explanation: From lateral to medial: Iliocostalis, Longissimus, Spinalis ('I Love Spaghetti'); erector spinae is the main extensor of the spine.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Muscles & Movemen.question: The transversospinalis muscles run from transverse processes to spinous processes and characteristically:
options: Rotate the spine to the opposite side and extend it
Rotate the spine to the same side and flex it
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Muscles & Movemen.explanation: Transversospinalis muscles (semispinalis, multifidus, rotatores) extend the spine and rotate it to the contralateral side; multifidus is a key lumbar stabiliser.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Muscles & Movemen.question: Bilateral contraction of splenius capitis produces ____; unilateral contraction produces ____.
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Muscles & Movemen.explanation: Splenius bilaterally extends the head/neck and unilaterally rotates the head to the SAME (ipsilateral) side.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Muscles & Movemen.question: Which muscle forms the MEDIAL border of the suboccipital triangle?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Muscles & Movemen.explanation: The suboccipital triangle is bounded medially by rectus capitis posterior major, laterally by obliquus capitis superior and inferiorly by obliquus capitis inferior.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Muscles & Movemen.question: The suboccipital triangle contains which important artery?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Muscles & Movemen.explanation: The third part of the vertebral artery runs in the floor of the suboccipital triangle before passing through the foramen magnum; it is vulnerable to injury on extreme rotation.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Muscles & Movemen.question: The suboccipital muscles are supplied by the:
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Muscles & Movemen.explanation: The suboccipital nerve (the posterior ramus of C1) supplies the four suboccipital muscles.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Muscles & Movemen.question: Flexion of the vertebral column is produced mainly by the:
options: Anterior abdominal muscles and psoas major
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Muscles & Movemen.explanation: The intrinsic back muscles are extensors; flexion of the trunk is produced by the anterior abdominal wall muscles and psoas major.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Muscles & Movemen.question: Rotation of the vertebral column is freest in which region?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Muscles & Movemen.explanation: The thoracic region permits the freest rotation because of its coronally-oriented facet joints (though the ribs limit total range); the lumbar region resists rotation.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Muscles & Movemen.question: The thoracolumbar fascia provides attachment for which two muscles, linking trunk and limb?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Muscles & Movemen.explanation: The thoracolumbar fascia anchors latissimus dorsi and transversus abdominis, helping transfer load between the trunk and upper/lower limbs.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Muscles & Movemen.question: A drooping shoulder with weak elevation after a posterior-triangle lymph node biopsy suggests injury to the:
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Muscles & Movemen.explanation: Accessory nerve (CN XI) injury denervates trapezius, causing a drooping shoulder and weak shoulder elevation/scapular retraction — a risk in posterior triangle surgery.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Muscles & Movemen.question: Extreme neck rotation or manipulation risks dissection of which artery in the suboccipital region?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Muscles & Movemen.explanation: The vertebral artery's third part is exposed in the suboccipital triangle and can be dissected by extreme rotation or manipulation, causing posterior circulation stroke.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Muscles & Movemen.question: Which muscle is a key segmental stabiliser of the lumbar spine, targeted in rehabilitation?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Muscles & Movemen.explanation: Multifidus (part of transversospinalis) is a key deep lumbar stabiliser and a focus of core/back-pain rehabilitation.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Muscles & Movemen.question: The serratus posterior superior and inferior muscles function as:
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Muscles & Movemen.explanation: The serratus posterior muscles (supplied by intercostal nerves) are accessory muscles of respiration.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Muscles & Movemen.question: Which of the following is an INTRINSIC (true) back muscle?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Muscles & Movemen.explanation: Erector spinae is an intrinsic back muscle (posterior rami); trapezius, latissimus dorsi, rhomboids and levator scapulae are extrinsic (move the limb).

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Spinal Cord & Men.question: In an adult, the spinal cord (conus medullaris) ends at approximately which level?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Spinal Cord & Men.explanation: The adult spinal cord ends at L1/L2 as the conus medullaris; the dural sac continues to S2.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Spinal Cord & Men.question: How many pairs of spinal nerves are there?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Spinal Cord & Men.explanation: There are 31 pairs of spinal nerves: 8 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral and 1 coccygeal.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Spinal Cord & Men.question: The lateral horn of spinal grey matter (T1–L2) contains:
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Spinal Cord & Men.explanation: The lateral horn (present T1–L2) contains the sympathetic preganglionic neuron cell bodies — the thoracolumbar sympathetic outflow.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Spinal Cord & Men.question: The cell bodies of primary sensory neurons are located in the:
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Spinal Cord & Men.explanation: Sensory neuron cell bodies lie in the dorsal root ganglion (DRG) on the dorsal root; the ventral root is purely motor.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Spinal Cord & Men.question: The dural sac (and subarachnoid space) ends at which level?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Spinal Cord & Men.explanation: The dural sac and subarachnoid space end at S2; the cord itself ends higher at L1/L2, leaving the lumbar cistern for safe LP.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Spinal Cord & Men.question: The epidural space contains fat and which venous structure?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Spinal Cord & Men.explanation: The epidural (extradural) space contains fat and the internal vertebral venous (Batson's) plexus; it is the target for epidural anaesthesia.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Spinal Cord & Men.question: The dorsal column–medial lemniscus pathway carries ____ and decussates in the ____.
options: fine touch, vibration and proprioception; medulla
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Spinal Cord & Men.explanation: The DCML carries fine touch, vibration and proprioception and decussates in the medulla (internal arcuate fibres).

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Spinal Cord & Men.question: The spinothalamic tract decussates:
options: At the level of the cord
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Spinal Cord & Men.explanation: The spinothalamic tract crosses at the cord level (within 1–2 segments, via the anterior white commissure) — hence contralateral pain/temperature loss in cord lesions.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Spinal Cord & Men.question: A cord hemisection causes ipsilateral touch/proprioception loss but contralateral pain/temperature loss because:
options: Both tracts cross in the medulla
The corticospinal tract crosses at the cord
Both tracts cross at the cord
The spinothalamic tract does not cross
DCML crosses in the medulla while spinothalamic crosses at the cord
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Spinal Cord & Men.explanation: DCML decussates high (medulla) so its loss is ipsilateral; the spinothalamic tract decussates low (cord) so its loss is contralateral — the basis of Brown-Séquard syndrome.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Spinal Cord & Men.question: The lateral corticospinal tract, carrying voluntary motor fibres, decussates in the:
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Spinal Cord & Men.explanation: About 85% of corticospinal fibres decussate in the medullary pyramids to form the lateral corticospinal tract.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Spinal Cord & Men.question: The anterior spinal artery supplies what proportion of the spinal cord?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Spinal Cord & Men.explanation: The single anterior spinal artery supplies the anterior two-thirds of the cord; the two posterior spinal arteries supply the posterior third (dorsal columns).

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Spinal Cord & Men.question: Anterior spinal artery syndrome characteristically SPARES which modality?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Spinal Cord & Men.explanation: The anterior spinal artery does not supply the dorsal columns, so proprioception and fine touch are spared while motor and pain/temperature are lost.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Spinal Cord & Men.question: The artery of Adamkiewicz most often arises on which side and at what level?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Spinal Cord & Men.explanation: The artery of Adamkiewicz (major anterior segmental medullary artery) usually arises on the left around T9–T12 and is a key supply to the lower cord.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Spinal Cord & Men.question: Which region of the spinal cord is a 'watershed' zone most vulnerable to ischaemia?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Spinal Cord & Men.explanation: The mid-thoracic cord (~T4–T9) is a watershed between vascular territories and is vulnerable to ischaemia, e.g. during aortic surgery.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Spinal Cord & Men.question: Brown-Séquard syndrome (cord hemisection) produces:
options: Loss of all modalities on one side
Ipsilateral motor/dorsal-column loss with contralateral pain/temperature loss
Bilateral pain loss with preserved motor
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Spinal Cord & Men.explanation: Brown-Séquard gives ipsilateral motor and dorsal-column (touch/proprioception) loss plus contralateral pain/temperature loss a few segments below the lesion.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Spinal Cord & Men.question: Subacute combined degeneration of the cord (vitamin B12 deficiency) affects which tracts?
options: Dorsal columns and lateral corticospinal tracts
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Spinal Cord & Men.explanation: B12 deficiency damages the dorsal columns and lateral corticospinal tracts, causing sensory ataxia with UMN signs.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Spinal Cord & Men.question: The cervical enlargement of the spinal cord supplies which region?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Spinal Cord & Men.explanation: The cervical enlargement (C5–T1) contains the motor and sensory neurons for the upper limb (brachial plexus).

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Spinal Cord & Men.question: The C8 spinal nerve exits the vertebral canal:
options: Below the C7 pedicle (between C7 and T1)
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Spinal Cord & Men.explanation: There are 8 cervical nerves but 7 cervical vertebrae; C1–C7 exit above their pedicle, and C8 exits below the C7 pedicle (between C7 and T1). From T1 down, each nerve exits below its numbered pedicle.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Vessels.question: The thoracic vertebrae and spinal cord receive their segmental blood supply mainly from the:
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Vessels.explanation: In the thoracic region the segmental spinal arteries are branches of the posterior intercostal arteries (from the aorta); the cervical region is supplied by the vertebral and ascending cervical arteries.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Vessels.question: The anterior spinal artery supplies which part of the spinal cord?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Vessels.explanation: The single anterior spinal artery supplies the anterior two-thirds of the cord; the two posterior spinal arteries supply the posterior third (dorsal columns).

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Vessels.question: How many anterior and posterior spinal arteries are there?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Vessels.explanation: There is one anterior spinal artery (in the anterior median fissure) and two posterior spinal arteries.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Vessels.question: The artery of Adamkiewicz most commonly arises on the ____ side at the ____ level.
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Vessels.explanation: The artery of Adamkiewicz (major anterior segmental medullary artery) usually arises on the left at T9–T12 and is a key supply to the lower cord.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Vessels.question: The mid-thoracic cord (~T4–T9) is clinically important because it is a:
options: Region supplied only by the posterior spinal arteries
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Vessels.explanation: The mid-thoracic cord is a watershed between vascular territories and is vulnerable to ischaemia, e.g. during aortic cross-clamping.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Vessels.question: Anterior spinal artery syndrome characteristically spares:
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Vessels.explanation: The anterior spinal artery does not supply the dorsal columns, so proprioception and fine touch are spared while motor and pain/temperature are lost.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Vessels.question: The internal vertebral venous plexus is located in the:
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Vessels.explanation: The internal vertebral venous plexus lies in the epidural space around the dura; the external plexus lies outside the vertebral column.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Vessels.question: Batson's vertebral venous plexus allows retrograde metastatic spread because it:
options: Is part of the portal system
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Vessels.explanation: The valveless plexus lets raised intra-abdominal/thoracic pressure divert blood (and tumour cells) into it, carrying prostate/breast cancer to the vertebrae and brain.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Vessels.question: Which cancers most classically metastasise to the vertebrae via Batson's plexus?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Vessels.explanation: Prostate and breast cancer (among others) spread to the spine via the valveless vertebral venous plexus, making vertebrae a common site of bony metastasis.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Vessels.question: The basivertebral veins drain which structure?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Vessels.explanation: The basivertebral veins emerge from the posterior surface of the vertebral body and drain it into the internal vertebral venous plexus.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Vessels.question: The vertebral artery ascends the neck by passing through the:
options: Foramina transversaria of C6 to C1
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Vessels.explanation: The vertebral artery ascends through the foramina transversaria of C6 up to C1, then crosses the suboccipital triangle to enter the foramen magnum.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Vessels.question: The vertebral artery is a branch of the:
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Vessels.explanation: The vertebral artery arises from the first part of the subclavian artery and unites with its fellow to form the basilar artery.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Vessels.question: Paraplegia after thoracoabdominal aortic aneurysm surgery is usually due to occlusion of the:
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Vessels.explanation: Interruption of the artery of Adamkiewicz during aortic surgery infarcts the anterior spinal artery territory, causing anterior cord syndrome and paraplegia.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Vessels.question: Less local anaesthetic is needed for an epidural in a pregnant patient because:
options: Epidural venous engorgement reduces the epidural space volume
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Vessels.explanation: In pregnancy, IVC compression engorges the vertebral venous plexus, reducing the epidural space volume so a smaller dose spreads further.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Vessels.question: A spinal epidural haematoma compressing the cord most often arises from bleeding of the:
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Vessels.explanation: Bleeding from the internal vertebral venous plexus (in the epidural space) can form a haematoma that compresses the spinal cord — a neurosurgical emergency.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Vessels.question: Vertebral artery dissection, often after neck manipulation, classically causes:
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Vessels.explanation: The vertebral artery supplies the posterior brain circulation, so its dissection causes brainstem/cerebellar (posterior circulation) stroke, often with occipital headache.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Vessels.question: The two posterior spinal arteries supply which part of the cord?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Vessels.explanation: The paired posterior spinal arteries supply the posterior third of the cord, including the dorsal columns; the anterior two-thirds is supplied by the anterior spinal artery.
